lead: An equation M dx + N dy = 0 is exact when its left side is the total differential of one function F(x, y). Then the solution is simply F(x, y) = C. The test is M<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>. Some equations fail the test but become exact after multiplying by a factor μ. This gives a direct route for equations that are not separable or homogeneous, and it appears in thermodynamics, circuit balance and potential problems.
prereq: You need order and degree, separable equations, homogeneous equations, partial derivatives and the total differential.

blocks.text: Write the equation as M(x, y) dx + N(x, y) dy = 0. M is the coefficient of dx; N is the coefficient of dy. The equation is exact if there is a function F(x, y) with Fx = M and Fy = N.
Then the left side is the total differential dF = F<sub>x</sub> dx + F<sub>y</sub> dy, so the equation says dF = 0. Its general solution is F(x, y) = C, where C is a constant.

The test follows in three lines. Suppose F has continuous second partials. If F exists, then M<sub>y</sub> = F<sub>xy</sub> = F<sub>yx</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>. So exactness requires M<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>. Here M<sub>y</sub> means ∂M/∂y and N<sub>x</sub> means ∂N/∂x. The converse also holds on a rectangle: when M<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>, such an F exists.

blocks.where: M<sub>y</sub> = ∂M/∂y; N<sub>x</sub> = ∂N/∂x; both partial derivatives are continuous.

blocks.text: Once the test passes, find F by integration. Two routes give the same F; use the one with easier integrals.

items: Integrate M with respect to x, treating y as a constant: F = ∫M dx + g(y). The function g(y) is the constant of integration, but here it may depend on y.
Differentiate this F with respect to y: F<sub>y</sub> = ∂/∂y(∫M dx) + g′(y). Set it equal to N.
Solve for g′(y). It must contain only y; if x remains, the equation was not exact or an integration slip occurred.
Integrate g′(y) to get g(y). Write F and the answer F(x, y) = C.

blocks.text: The mirror route integrates N with respect to y first, giving F = ∫N dy + h(x), and finds h′(x) from M. End every solution with a check: differentiate your F. Fx must equal M and Fy must equal N. This catches a wrong g(y) and a sign error. The answer is a family of curves, one curve for each C. An initial condition fixes C, as in 1.7.

When My ≠ Nx, try to multiply the whole equation by a nonzero function μ(x, y). The new equation μM dx + μN dy = 0 is exact if (μM)y = (μN)x. The function μ is an integrating factor. Two standard rules cover many exam problems.

items: Rule 1. Compute R = (M<sub>y</sub> − N<sub>x</sub>)/N, with N ≠ 0. If R depends on x alone, then μ(x) = e<sup>∫R dx</sup>.
Rule 2. Compute S = (N<sub>x</sub> − M<sub>y</sub>)/M, with M ≠ 0. If S depends on y alone, then μ(y) = e<sup>∫S dy</sup>.
In each rule, first simplify R or S. If the result still contains both x and y, that rule does not apply. Multiply both M and N by μ, then repeat the exactness test.

blocks.text: For simple combinations, grouping is faster than the rules. Learn this table.
Other integrating factors exist. For a homogeneous equation with xM + yN ≠ 0, μ = 1/(xM + yN) works; only a few universities teach that one. See 1.5 for the linear-equation integrating factor e∫P dx.

figure.caption: The test splits the work: equality leads straight to F(x, y) = C; inequality sends the equation through an integrating factor μ and then the same exact integration.

spec.title: Exact or make it exact
spec.aria: A flowchart tests M_y against N_x and branches to the direct integral or to multiplying by an integrating factor.

examples.question: Solve each equation and find the constant C in F(x, y) = C. (a) (2xy + y²)dx + (x² + 2xy)dy = 0 with y(1) = 2. (b) (3xy + y²)dx + (x² + xy)dy = 0 with y(1) = 1.
steps: M<sub>y</sub> = 2x + 2y and N<sub>x</sub> = 2x + 2y, so the equation is exact.
F<sub>y</sub> = x² + 2xy + g′(y). Set F<sub>y</sub> = N: x² + 2xy + g′(y) = x² + 2xy, so g′(y) = 0 and g is constant.
M<sub>y</sub> = 3x + 2y and N<sub>x</sub> = 2x + y, not equal.
(M<sub>y</sub> − N<sub>x</sub>)/N = (x + y)/(x² + xy) = 1/x, a function of x alone, so μ = e<sup>∫dx/x</sup> = x.
μ = x is nonzero only for x ≠ 0, so the curve x = 0 must be checked separately against the original equation.
Now M<sub>y</sub> = 3x² + 2xy = N<sub>x</sub>, so it is exact.
F<sub>y</sub> = x³ + x²y + g′(y) = x³ + x²y, so g′ = 0.
examples.answer: The constants are C = 6 for part (a) and C = 1.5 for part (b); no units are involved.

traps: The test is M<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>, not M<sub>x</sub> = N<sub>y</sub>. The variables are crossed: differentiate M by y and N by x.
An integrating factor multiplies both M and N. Multiplying only one changes the equation and usually destroys exactness.
After integrating M with respect to x, the constant of integration is a function g(y), not a number. Dropping g(y) loses terms that may contain y only.

In Rule 2 the numerator order is N<sub>x</sub> − M<sub>y</sub>. Reversing the order gives S′ = −S, so the integrating factor becomes e<sup>−∫S dy</sup> = 1/μ, not −μ. Both work, but pick one order and keep it.
Always re-test after multiplying by μ. A μ from a rule that only nearly fits can still leave the equation inexact.

quiz.q: State the necessary and sufficient criterion for M dx + N dy = 0 to be exact on a rectangle.
quiz.a: The equation is exact when M<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>x</sub>, with continuous first partials.

quiz.q: Why does an exact equation have the solution F(x, y) = C?
quiz.a: Exactness gives F<sub>x</sub> = M and F<sub>y</sub> = N. Then M dx + N dy = dF, so the equation is dF = 0. Integrating gives F(x, y) = C.
M = 2xy + 3, N = x² − 4y. M<sub>y</sub> = 2x and N<sub>x</sub> = 2x. They are equal, so the equation is exact.
F = ∫(2xy + 3)dx = x²y + 3x + g(y). F<sub>y</sub> = x² + g′(y) = x² − 4y, so g′(y) = −4y and g(y) = −2y². Solution: x²y + 3x − 2y² = C.
M<sub>y</sub> = 3x + 4y, N<sub>x</sub> = 2x + 2y. R = (M<sub>y</sub> − N<sub>x</sub>)/N = (x + 2y)/(x² + 2xy) = 1/x. So μ = e<sup>∫dx/x</sup> = x.

quiz.q: For an equation, (N<sub>x</sub> − M<sub>y</sub>)/M = 2y. Find μ and state which variable it depends on.
quiz.a: This is Rule 2 with S = 2y, which depends on y alone. μ = e<sup>∫2y dy</sup> = e<sup>y²</sup>. It depends on y.

quiz.q: Write the exact differential equal to (x dy − y dx)/x².

beyond: Not for the exam. Exactness is the two-variable case of a closed differential form being exact; in thermodynamics, internal energy is exact while heat and work are not. Search 'inexact differentials', 'integrating factor thermodynamics', and 'potential function criterion'. Numerical solvers sometimes use conservative or symplectic integrators that preserve such structure.
